changes.old: None computed. Second-hand figures: methamphetamine raises the likelihood of intracerebral haemorrhage by as much as 2–5 times (refs 11, 37: Huang et al.; Westover et al.; no intervals); among people who used methamphetamine in Huang et al., incidence of subarachnoid haemorrhage 6.2 and of intracerebral haemorrhage 20.8 per 100,000 person-years (no comparison-group rates given); aneurysmal haemorrhage outcomes worse with methamphetamine: median Glasgow Outcome Score 3 versus 5 at discharge (p<0.001; Beadell), OR 5 (95% CI 1.03 to 24) at 1 year and OR 7.2 (1.2 to 30) at 3 years (Moon); ischaemic stroke subtypes in users versus non-users 31% vs 28% small-vessel, 25% vs 24% large-vessel, 34% vs 46% cardioembolic (not significant; Zhu 2023); ventricular thrombus in 10 of 30 people with methamphetamine cardiomyopathy (Schürer); QTc prolongation in 27% of 158 people who used methamphetamine (Haning & Goebert); 86% higher risk of a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation in a 2022 California database analysis; relapse in 61% of 350 people within a year of treatment (Brecht & Herbeck).

changes.old: The commentary and summary are causal and categorical in a way the cited evidence is not: methamphetamine is said to damage dopaminergic neurotransmission and to preferentially cause psychiatric complications, chronic use to have "devastating effects" on the central nervous system, and users to have deficits in memory and executive function, with no comparison figures and no acknowledgment that the cross-sectional studies behind these statements cannot separate pre-existing differences from drug effects (a possibility the body itself raises twice). The Key Points state that dopamine receptor antagonists are the most effective treatments for the chronic psychiatric manifestations, which no trial in the review supports: the body cites one 1974 study of a neuroleptic against amphetamine-induced symptoms and a 1992 hypothesis paper on formication. The statement that about 40% of people who use methamphetamine have abnormalities on neuropsychiatric tests is traced here to a study of people with HIV. Where the review is at its best is the Parkinson's section, where the hypotheses are set against each other and the weakness of the positive studies is named.

changes.old: Parkinson's disease: the author states the prevailing view is that methamphetamine use does not raise the risk, supported by four arguments: methamphetamine affects dopaminergic terminals rather than substantia nigra cell bodies; reductions are greater in the caudate than the putamen, the reverse of Parkinson's disease; transporter reductions recovered significantly after more than 12 months of abstinence; and vesicular monoamine transporter binding, which is reduced in Parkinson's disease and resistant to compensatory regulation, was not reduced in abstinent users and was increased in one study of people not abstinent.
